Being around people is exhausting for me. It's not even that I don't like them, it just naturally drains my energy. So, my way of coping: 1. Make sure you obtain enough solitude, otherwise you'll quickly grow into a grumpy asshole who hates everyone. 2. People tend me self involved, so you don't have to make conversation. Ask questions, and just listen. Then ask a follow up question, and say things that loosely seem you relate (I would love that; how cool; I can't imagine; if that was me, damn!). 3. Eye contact. It's weird, but if you maintain eye contact the other person will do the heavy lifting in the conversation...and you might just get a bit lost in it as well.

Just pretend everyone is an old friend you've known all your life and just do you. It doesn't matter how long you stretch out the getting to know you process, if they don't like you... They don't like you. It's fine to not like someone.

There is nothing wrong with being an introvert..embrace it. Introverts have great qualities and are often good judges of character as they take the time to observe others. If you struggle to fit in at work just mimic the inane and superficial things that usually get said in a work environment and you'll fit in ok. The worst thing you can do in a work place is tell anyone anything personal about yourself as it will probably get gossiped about and come back to bite you in the ass. If you have to, just make shit up.Ie what did you do on the weekend? Caught up with friends and then ask back what did you do.Most other people love to talk about themselves.

Be polite and honest. Someone wants you to go out somewhere, honestly tell them that's not your thing and you'd rather have a relaxing night in. Be open about what you enjoy doing and who you are.

When you do have to interact with people, try an observation mode that's part 'strong and silent type' and part grandparent. Let them do their thing and just enjoy their enjoyment. Basically try being the embodiment of that moment when two guys look at each other from across the room and give a little nod.

Listen to understand, rather than listening to respond.

If you're constantly thinking about what you're going to say, you can't pay them attention. When it's your turn to talk, the things you say betray whether you understand where the conversation is headed or if you're just trying to dump your opinion on them.

 

Examples, for those who don't already know what I'm talking about:

Let's say you've just met a brother of a close friend. He's kinda lonely so he's really interested in socializing. He's talking about his hobby, cars and mechanical shit, when something he says reminds you of a guy you once knew who lost a finger to an engine. Now that's potentially a great story, losing a finger to an engine. But if he's talking about the effects of different arrangements of the cylinders, it's probably not appropriate to bring up at the moment.

Now, if he talks about some kind of bodily harm, like dropping a 7/8" wrench on his manhood, then you can add the story about a man whose engine ate his finger. That's within the overall topic and it doesn't sound like you're forcing the story, but merely relating it because it's relevant. You're engaging in the conversation that he wants to have. He'll like you more because of that.

 

Make the small talk count.

Small talk can be really hard for some. For those that have mastered it without any prior talent in the subject, they have done so by trial and error. Just start asking things about the person, using their appearance as a guide. If they have tattoos, maybe start talking about tattoos you've seen and liked, and segue into what their tattoos mean. If they have eyeglasses that are obviously thick, ask them about how bad their vision is. Most people with awful vision like to complain about it. If it was rude, take that hit and move on. You can't learn any other way.

Some people hate small talk, and appreciate when you don't do it. They'd rather talk about large, important things with strangers than the Cubs game last night or the weather. Personally, I always start off with one of these topics as a litmus test to see if the person I'm trying to smalltalk prefers this kind of a conversation. I'll say something like "I can't believe there are places in the world where it's okay to marry 6 year olds." and if they get put off, I switch it up with an 'acceptable' topic.

Some people just really want to complain. Mothers of young children particularly, or anyone carrying something heavy or waiting for an extended period of time. I'll say something (to the moms) along the lines of "You know, if you cover their mouths with duct tape you can save on earplugs and groceries." Don't try and be PC if you think someone wants to complain. Your apparent carelessness about the societal rules will encourage them to open up, since complaining isn't really PC either (unless it's against Trump, I guess).
